conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. I’d like to use a quick, well-trusted tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s just ten short questions that ask about things like mood, anxiety, sleep, and appetite over the past seven days. There are no “right” or “wrong” answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me something that makes us worry about safety, in which case we’ll work together on next steps. Ready when you are; we’ll take it one question at a time.

To start: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*(soft sigh)*  
Honestly… most of the time it feels pretty hard. My husband will make a joke or I’ll see something on my phone that used to make me giggle, and I just… can’t. I might force a little smile so he doesn’t worry, but inside I still feel flat. Only once or twice in the past week did I actually laugh, and even then it faded right away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… most days I can’t. A couple of times I managed a little laugh, but it felt forced and it disappeared right away. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of dull now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

No… I haven’t. Even simple stuff—like my favorite show coming on or a friend dropping by—just feels like another chore. I used to get excited about little plans, but this week it’s like, “What’s the point?” I still do them, but the happy anticipation isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every little thing I did, convinced it was my fault. I know rationally babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing her somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly think, “What if she stops breathing?” or I’ll hear a siren and imagine it’s headed to the hospital because something’s wrong with her. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the doctor says she’s doing great—but the thoughts just crash in. I can usually talk myself down after a while, but it keeps happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a tight wave rolls over me—my heart races and I feel kind of shaky, even if I’m just sitting on the couch. There’s nothing dangerous happening, but for a minute or two it feels like something awful is about to. It passes if I do some deep breaths, but it’s happened maybe three times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, I drop everything to soothe her, and then the mess just piles up. By the afternoon I’m staring at the dishes or the laundry hill and thinking, “I’ll never get through this.” I still manage the basics—she’s fed, I’m fed—but it feels like I’m constantly behind and one step from drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head just keeps spinning—thinking I didn’t do enough today, worrying something might be wrong with her, replaying every cry. It takes me forever to nod off, and then I jerk awake at every little sound she makes. I’m sleeping maybe four broken hours a night, if that.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest that won’t lift. Even when the baby smiles, the sadness is still sitting right behind it. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, but mostly I just feel empty or on the verge of tears.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocker with her asleep on my chest and tears started rolling—no real trigger, just this ache that overflowed. It’s maybe three or four times this week; I try to keep it quiet so my partner doesn’t worry, but the tears come whether I want them to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds as though the joy you once found in everyday moments has slipped away since your baby arrived; instead of excitement you feel weighed down by constant worry, nightly tears, and a sense that you are somehow failing as a mum. You are doing your very best-getting her fed, keeping her safe-yet you describe feeling overwhelmed, unable to laugh or look forward to things, and haunted by frightening "what-ifs" about her health.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response describes inability to laugh, forced laughter, and loss of humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory joy, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for normal infant behaviors, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive, catastrophic worries occurring daily without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected episodes of intense physical anxiety (racing heart, shakiness) with dread, occurring 3× in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to keep up, and feeling close to 'drowning,' matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent worries and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes pervasive daily sadness, emotional heaviness, and persistent emptiness despite positive moments, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying 3–4 times this week without a clear trigger, which aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the EPDS threshold of 14 that flags probable major depression. You endorsed core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: pervasive low mood and loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) most of the time, accompanied by marked guilt, anxiety, sleep impairment, and functional difficulty managing daily tasks. Although you denied self-harm thoughts today, the overall symptom load indicates an urgent need for formal psychiatric evaluation and support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>GP</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment (therapy and/or antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding if applicable)
3. Plan daily 30-minute mood check-ins with a trusted adult; share EPDS result so they can help monitor
4. Encourage 4-5 hour combined sleep blocks; consider partner/family night-time shifts and safe cosleeping guidelines
5. Limit self-blame: keep a brief log of daily "small wins" (e.g., shower, meal) to counter negative self-talk
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress once treatment begins
7. If distress escalates or self-harm thoughts emerge, go to nearest emergency department or call emergency services
8. Provide phone numbers for 24/7 support lines such as PANDA (Postpartum Depression & Anxiety) or local crisis services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report; responses indicate moderate–severe symptom severity.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding parenting adequacy  
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety, panic-like episodes (≈3×/week)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties related to ruminative worry  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in daily tasks  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days this week,” causing functional impairment but without self-harm ideation (explicitly denied).

Screening significance  
Meets threshold indicators for possible major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; suicidal ideation absent on today’s screen. Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR) and safety-planning follow-up within 1 week.
